video_title: Stocks Plunge After the Midterms. Can Bitcoin Survive the AI Selloff?
gist: Bankless weekly rollup: a post-midterm Democratic sweep coincided with a sharp AI-infrastructure-led equity selloff (S&P -4%, Nasdaq -6%, SOXX -12%) while Bitcoin clung to its ~$76K 50-week moving average after surviving the $6.34B North Korean Binance hack. The hosts expect Democrats to target Trump-linked crypto and stablecoin yield rather than the whole industry, and also cover a French bank hack exiting via crypto, Ethereum's accelerated post-quantum roadmap, and bearish insider-selling plans at Coinbase.

insights.claim: In roughly a day and a half after the 2026 midterms, the S&P 500 fell about 4% (back to June 2026 levels) and the Nasdaq/QQQ fell about 6% (back to April 2026 levels), the worst decline since around 2018.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Broad index drawdown erased the post-midterm rally entirely.
insights.quote: in the last just day and a half of trading, the S&P is down 4%. 4% is just gargantuan for the S&P.

insights.claim: The selloff was concentrated in AI build-out names: the SOXX semiconductor index fell 12%, Nvidia 8.6%, Intel 7% (61% off all-time highs), and Micron 14% on the day (45% off highs), while the State Street tech ETF fell 7%.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Semis and memory are the epicenter; AI capex suppliers carry the most downside beta.
insights.quote: Semiconductors SOXX is down 12% just an index of semiconductors.

insights.claim: AI spenders and mega-cap platforms were buffered relative to AI suppliers: Amazon fell 2% but was flat on the week, Google fell 1.5% and had held since earnings, and Apple stayed near all-time highs.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Market is discriminating between AI capex buyers (resilient) and AI capex sellers (punished) - a pair-trade signal.
insights.quote: So, the AI infrastructure buildout companies are just getting absolutely walloped.

insights.claim: David frames the move as the AI bubble popping, arguing the AI tech selloff predated the midterms and simply resumed once the election left the spotlight.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Election was a distraction from an ongoing AI-sector derating, not its cause.
insights.quote: now that midterms are in the rearview mirror, actually, people still want to sell tech stocks, I guess.

insights.claim: The co-host pushes back that it is too early on Thursday to call an AI bubble pop and views it as a correction after tremendous gains, returning indices only to summertime levels.
insights.speaker: Co-host (Ryan)
insights.so_what: Counterview: drawdown is mean reversion in context of the year's gains.
insights.quote: I would say still too early on this Thursday to call this an AI bubble pop. It does seem like a correction.

insights.claim: Markets whipsawed on the Democratic sweep: initially hating it, rallying the day after, then posting heavy selling Thursday, with the VIX reportedly hitting 2018-like highs.
insights.speaker: Co-host (Ryan)
insights.so_what: Sentiment is swinging between extremes in 24-hour increments, signaling a high-volatility regime.
insights.quote: the VIX is hitting like 2018 highs, but we are whipsawing from like oh we're so back to it's so over in 24hour increments.

insights.claim: Assets tied to Trump and Elon Musk sold off specifically on the blue wave: Trump Media fell about 30%, the Trump memecoin fell about 30%, and Tesla and SpaceX declined while everything else was rallying post-midterms because Democrats are targeting Musk.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Political-proximity assets are the clean expression of the election outcome.
insights.quote: Tesla SpaceX were down bigly just because Democrats are going after Elon.

insights.claim: Historically, a Republican president paired with a Democrat-controlled House and Senate has been followed by solid stock returns at 3, 6, 9 and 12 months, because markets like gridlock.
insights.speaker: Co-host (Ryan)
insights.so_what: Divided government base rate argues against extrapolating the selloff.
insights.quote: Markets have traditionally liked that. They sort of like the standoff.

insights.claim: Democrats swept both chambers in the 2026 midterms, with the Senate flipping to about 54 Democratic senators and the House also flipping, attributed by the hosts to unpopular war, rising energy prices and CPI, and Trump neglecting affordability.
insights.speaker: Co-host (Ryan)
insights.so_what: Unified Democratic Congress against a Republican president sets up gridlock and oversight fights.
insights.quote: 54 senators elected, I think two other seats in contention.

insights.claim: David expects Democrats to seek retribution against Trump-linked crypto (Trump memecoin, WLFI, Trump Media) for using crypto as a 'grifty piggy bank', but not to crack down on the whole industry as under Gensler.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Trump-family crypto assets carry policy risk; broader crypto less so.
insights.quote: I think that Democrats are going to come and like seek retribution for Trump using the crypto industry as his grifty piggy bank

insights.claim: A likely risk is a 'round two' on the Clarity Act in which banks lobby Maxine Waters and Elizabeth Warren to revise it in their favor, specifically to restrict stablecoin yield.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Stablecoin yield economics (e.g., for issuers/exchanges) is the most exposed policy lever.
insights.quote: What I do think is on the table is that the banks get a second attempt at stable coin yield with the Clarity Act.

insights.claim: Both hosts argue Democrats have bigger fish to fry in AI and data centers, predicting Elizabeth Warren's new cause will be an 'anti-data center army' rather than an anti-crypto army.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Political heat shifts from crypto to AI infrastructure - another headwind for data-center build-out names.
insights.quote: I think it'll be an anti-data center army that Elizabeth Warren and

insights.claim: Unlike 2022-2023, big Wall Street funders of Democrats such as BlackRock now see opportunity in tokenization and are full steam ahead on crypto, reducing the incentive for Democrats to stall the industry.
insights.speaker: Co-host (Ryan)
insights.so_what: Incumbent financial lobby alignment lowers the odds of a hostile crypto regime.
insights.quote: ironically, you have kind of like big asset manager Wall Street sort of on the side of crypto and that's different than it was in 2022, 2023.

insights.claim: Maxine Waters' early proposal, a 'crypto investor Bill of Rights', includes exchange withdrawals within 24 hours, segregated customer assets, bankruptcy remoteness and monthly proof of reserves, which the hosts consider reasonable and already the industry's direction.
insights.speaker: Co-host (Ryan)
insights.so_what: Initial Democratic asks are mild consumer-protection measures, not existential.
insights.quote: all exchange withdrawals uh have to happen within 24 hours, customer assets segregated, bankruptcy, remote, monthly proof of reserves.

insights.claim: David calls the purge of Trump-linked crypto grift a 'rough but necessary exorcism' that removes a constraint on crypto's upside, so long as Democrats leave Paul Atkins at the SEC and Mike Selig at the CFTC alone.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Bull case hinges on regulator continuity; watch for congressional pressure on SEC/CFTC leadership.
insights.quote: This is probably a rough but necessary necessary exorcism for the crypto industry to get rid of sort of Trump.

insights.claim: The co-host cautions it is unclear whether Democrats take the benign path or revert to broad anti-crypto policy, and that headline events like the $6B Binance hack make it impossible for legislators not to weigh in.
insights.speaker: Co-host (Ryan)
insights.so_what: Hacks raise the political salience of crypto and the tail risk of hostile legislation.

themes.theme: Bitcoin market structure and the 50-week MA

insights.claim: Bitcoin rose above $80,000 (nearly $81,000) after the midterms, then set a marginal new local low around $75,500, trading near $76,000 at recording, essentially sitting on its 50-week moving average (~$75.9K-76K).
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: BTC is testing a key cycle support level in real time.
insights.quote: now we have set a new low just a smidge of a new low but a new low nonetheless of 75,500.

insights.claim: The hosts treat the 50-week moving average as the key early-bull-cycle support level (citing Galaxy's Alex Thorn and Michael Nadeau of The DeFi Report), noting that in prior early bull cycles BTC always stayed above it.
insights.speaker: Co-host (Ryan)
insights.so_what: A decisive break below ~$76K would invalidate the early-bull-cycle framing.
insights.quote: In previous um early bull cycles, we've always stayed above that.

insights.claim: Crypto held up relatively well: Bitcoin fell about 2-3% on the week while ETH was roughly flat and did not set a new low, and Zcash held its own.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Relative strength in ETH and ZEC during an equity rout.
insights.quote: Bitcoin set a new local low. ETH did not.

insights.claim: David reads Bitcoin's quick recovery from the Binance hack (only a $3-4K drop versus an expected 15-20% decline) as evidence of strong market structure and remains net bullish despite the AI selloff.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Resilience to a worst-case headline suggests sellers are exhausted.
insights.quote: I would expect to be down like 15%, down 20% on Bitcoin in the week, and yet we recovered.

insights.claim: The co-host flags the downside scenario that the AI selloff continues, BTC breaks through the 50-week MA, and Ben Cowen is proven right with a new low.
insights.speaker: Co-host (Ryan)
insights.so_what: Keep the bear case live; position sizing around the MA matters.
insights.quote: You know, Ben Cowan could be right. We could go set like a new actual low low.

themes.theme: Binance $6B North Korea hack and laundering

insights.claim: North Korea's TraderTraitor (Lazarus) group stole about $6.34B from a Binance hot wallet, per an FBI alert - the largest heist in history and roughly 3-4x the ~$1.5B Bybit hack a year earlier.
insights.speaker: Co-host (Ryan)
insights.so_what: The long-feared top-exchange hack has happened; scale of state-actor theft keeps rising.
insights.quote: The largest bank heist in human history, $6.34 billion dollars, hacked by North Korea.

insights.claim: About $2.85B was frozen, mainly stablecoins: $1.77B of Tether, Circle USDC, $40M by Ripple (unusual), WLFI's freeze function, and Arbitrum froze 8,426 ETH and 74M ARB.
insights.speaker: Co-host (Ryan)
insights.so_what: Freezable assets (stablecoins, governed L2s) materially limit hack losses - a feature for users.
insights.quote: $2.85 billion was frozen and intercepted mainly USDC and USDT.

insights.claim: Binance covered the full ~$6.3B loss using its SAFU insurance fund (around $1B) plus balance-sheet funds, bought back the assets, and published proof of reserves, which calmed markets and limited BTC's drop to about 5%.
insights.speaker: Co-host (Ryan)
insights.so_what: Unlike FTX, a solvent exchange with transparent reserves contained contagion.
insights.quote: Binance came out though and they said they would they would uh provide coverage for the full 6 billion.

insights.claim: The attack vector was social engineering: a fake job interview gave a Binance employee a coding task that was malware, which spread across the internal network to a machine with private keys; attackers then abused EIP-7702 in Binance's smart contract wallet to bypass the normal withdrawal process. Infiltration was first detected in July.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Human/endpoint security, not cryptography, is the weak link; AI likely amplified the tooling.
insights.quote: They set up a fake job interview with a Binance employee.

insights.claim: Funds were laundered through ThorChain (TRX and Solana in, BTC and ETH out); unlike Tornado Cash, ThorChain has identifiable node operators, and the FBI explicitly named ThorChain node operators asking them not to process North Korean transactions.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Semi-decentralized protocols with 'buttons' face direct regulatory/legal exposure.
insights.quote: the FBI sent out an alert explicitly naming ThorChain node operators

insights.claim: David's framework: if a protocol has a button and can be regulated to push it, the state will compel it to; ThorChain sits in a 'squishy middle' between immutable code like Tornado Cash and governable chains, which he finds legally precarious.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Either fully decentralize or accept censorship obligations; the middle is the riskiest place to be.
insights.quote: So the only answer is to go fully decentralized and not have the ability to do these types of things.

insights.claim: David speculates ThorChain node operators avoid FBI action because they are cooperating and passing RPC-level tracing data to the FBI.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Speculation only; explains the absence of enforcement against operators.
insights.quote: That's my only explanation is that the four chain operators are narks.

insights.claim: Hacks are a significant double-digit percentage of North Korea's GDP and its number one revenue source funding its missile program, so the co-host argues the US may go on the offensive or offer private 10% recovery bounties.
insights.speaker: Co-host (Ryan)
insights.so_what: Possible future headline: mysteriously restored hack funds.
insights.quote: it's like these hacks are a significant double digit percentage of North Korea GDP and it's going right into their missile program.

insights.claim: Polygon validators froze about 6.5M POL (from the Binance and a Polymarket hack) and a proposal would roll back the chain - the biggest rollback since the DAO; hackers tried bribing validators with a ~20K fee transaction and side cash, but none defected.
insights.speaker: Co-host (Ryan)
insights.so_what: Governable chains are increasingly acting as recovery backstops.
insights.quote: So, this would be the biggest roll back since the DAO,

insights.claim: There is a clear split between immutable chains that cannot roll back (Bitcoin, Ethereum, Zcash) and chains like Arbitrum and Polygon that freeze or roll back, which some users may view as a feature; Arbitrum is 'two for two' saving funds in Bybit and Binance hacks.
insights.speaker: Co-host (Ryan)
insights.so_what: Chain choice is becoming a trade-off between credible neutrality and recoverability.
insights.quote: I think there's a clear split between chains that are completely immutable that will never cannot roll back.

themes.theme: TradFi bank hacked with crypto exit

insights.claim: French co-op bank Credit Mutual (about $200B balance sheet, 5.5M customers, 10,000+ employees) was digitally robbed of an estimated ~$130M after hackers entered via a third-party vendor system.
insights.speaker: Co-host (Ryan)
insights.so_what: Disproves the assumption that reversible TradFi rails make banks immune to heists.
insights.quote: they were robbed estimated it's not fully reported about $130 million.

insights.claim: The hackers sent SWIFT messages to networks of mule accounts at smaller banks, which pushed fiat to mule accounts at crypto exchanges (Kraken, Crypto.com, OKX), converted to stablecoins, and moved on-chain into bearer assets.
insights.speaker: Co-host (Ryan)
insights.so_what: Crypto is the getaway car; exchanges' fiat on-ramp KYC is the chokepoint regulators will target.
insights.quote: Kraken, Crypto.com, OKX mule accounts in these crypto exchanges that then move the fiat from fiat into stable coins.

insights.claim: On-chain sleuth ZachXBT flagged $106M of suspicious flows on November 2nd, possibly before the bank itself noticed.
insights.speaker: Co-host (Ryan)
insights.so_what: On-chain transparency can detect TradFi breaches faster than banks.
insights.quote: He saw it on chain November 2nd before maybe even the bank noticed that this was happening and he flagged $106 million.

insights.claim: David argues crypto's security practices are already a generation ahead of banks because bearer assets forced hardening, whereas banks relied on reversibility and likely have many holes via third-party tools; he asks whether this is a repeatable AI-enabled attack strategy.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Bank cybersecurity spend and vendor-risk scrutiny likely to rise; potential tail risk of a multi-billion US bank breach.
insights.quote: our defensive practices are already like a generation ahead of the banks.

themes.theme: Ethereum Devcon 8: post-quantum roadmap and focus

insights.claim: At Devcon 8 in Mumbai, Justin Drake announced a material update to Ethereum's strawmap targeting full post-quantum L1 (execution, consensus and data layers) by the 'J' fork, with Glamsterdam on mainnet in January 2027 and the full post-quantum/post-AI transition by December 2028 - leaving 24 months for three forks.
insights.speaker: Co-host (Ryan)
insights.so_what: Accelerated PQ timeline reduces quantum tail risk for ETH relative to slower chains.
insights.quote: our hope is that by December 2028 we'll be able to wrap up the full postquantum and postAI uh transition which gives us 24 months to ship the three forks after Glamsterdam.

insights.claim: Drake said leanVM reached end-to-end formal verification, and the timeline acceleration is driven by quantum attack progress and AI breakthroughs in math.
insights.speaker: Co-host (Ryan)
insights.so_what: AI-assisted formal verification is making faster protocol shipping credible.
insights.quote: LEINVM over the last few days and hours has reached a very significant milestone of end to end formal verification.

insights.claim: Gnosis Chain plans to become the first 'Ethereum Economic Zone' rollup tapping L1 liquidity by around spring next year, with demos like CoW Swap tapping mainnet liquidity; L2s with their own distribution like Robinhood and Coinbase's chain likely won't join.
insights.speaker: Co-host (Ryan)
insights.so_what: A cohort of ETH-aligned L2s may accrue value to ETH rather than compete.

insights.claim: L2Beat rebranded to ETHBeat, reflecting that L2s are no longer the main intermediaries between users and Ethereum and broadening its watchdog mandate to L1 intermediaries like node providers and smart contracts.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Signals the ecosystem's pivot back toward L1 scaling.

insights.claim: Vitalik's ~15-minute Devcon keynote mentioned Ethereum once and DeFi not at all, focusing on d/acc topics (trustworthy health devices, user-controlled social media, treating personal data as toxic waste); Georgios of Paradigm criticized it, and the hosts see it as Vitalik taking a different leadership role and a lack of focus on ETH the asset.
insights.speaker: Co-host (Ryan)
insights.so_what: Narrative/leadership focus remains a soft spot for ETH versus single-purpose assets like Zcash.
insights.quote: I'm pretty sure for ETH a goddamn asset which was not mentioned at all in the DevCon keynote.

insights.claim: Despite criticism, Paradigm shipped Solar, a 100x faster Solidity compiler, illustrating the hidden bullishness of deep developer talent on the EVM stack; Devcon attendance and energy were reportedly lower than prior years.
insights.speaker: Co-host (Ryan)
insights.so_what: EVM tooling momentum persists even amid community malaise.
insights.quote: Georgios and Paradigm shipped Solar which is 100x faster solidity.

themes.theme: Coinbase earnings and insider selling; Strategy

insights.claim: Coinbase's trading revenue was $590M, flat quarter over quarter, as prediction markets offset a 10% drop in spot volume; consumer spot volume is down 60% year over year, subscriptions and services are 49% of net revenue, and stablecoin revenue was $37M.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Retail spot activity is collapsing; Coinbase is leaning on prediction markets and subscriptions.
insights.quote: Uh consumer spot volume on Coinbase is down 60% year-over-year.

insights.claim: Brian Armstrong filed a 10b5-1 plan allowing him to sell 24% of his Coinbase shares (about 3% of total supply) at specific price targets, versus Vlad Tenev's plan to sell only 4% of his Robinhood shares; Armstrong owns about 8.5% of Coinbase and Tenev about 5.2% of Robinhood.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Founder-CEO's direction of travel is negative for COIN sentiment.
insights.quote: Brian Armstrong has filed giving himself the option to sh sell 24% of his shares at specific price targets.

insights.claim: With Coinbase stock down 60-70% from all-time highs and at a 970-day low, the hosts view the CEO raising his potential sales as a bearish signal; they would rather see insider buying. Coinbase has underperformed the rest of crypto on the year.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Avoid/underweight COIN signal from hosts.
insights.quote: it's kind of just a downer to see the stock down 60%, it's at 970day low

insights.claim: Strategy's STRC (Stretch) preferred briefly regained its $100 peg after 174 days off it, enabling ATM issuance, but significant convertible debt comes due over the next 6-9 months and MSTR is below conversion thresholds, so Saylor will need cash.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Upcoming convert maturities are a potential forced-funding overhang for MSTR and BTC.
insights.quote: It was off the peg for $174 days.
